newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Kohl cheers allies by vowing to run again in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Kohl cheers allies by vowing to run again in 1998.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl cheered his party and coalition partners on Thursday with a surprise announcement that he planned to stand for re-election in 1998 for an unprecedented fifth term.

Kohl, celebrating his 67th birthday and under pressure from economic ills as never before in his 14-year tenure, said he felt an obligation to run again in the next general election in late 1998 because of the challenges Germany faced.

In an interview with ARD national television during his Easter holiday in the Austrian resort of Bad Hofgastein, Kohl said he wanted to play a role in NATO's expansion, European integration and the launch of the planned European Union single currency.

"I have thought about this very carefully here, the path I have taken in these years and the burdens and the challenges," Kohl said. "I will stand again because I believe I have an obligation to do this in the current situation."

The news put an end to speculation that Kohl no longer had the stomach to face soaring unemployment, the need for painful welfare cuts to meet the criteria for European monetary union, and the challenge of instituting long-delayed structural reform.

The man seen as Kohl's most likely successor, Christian Democrat (CDU) parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, said that "especially in a time of difficult social upheavals, important political decisions and significant foreign policy changes, Germany needs a chancellor with authority and the ability to get things done".
"This is a good decision for Germany."

And some of the hopeful younger generation of CDU leaders, who earlier this year seemed to show Kohl was losing his grip on the party when they dared to question his leadership, made clear they still saw him as their best guarantee of election success.
"Helmut Kohl is the driving force of the CDU," Hamburg CDU boss Ole van Beust told the Berlin daily B.Z. "Even if we have had differences of opinion, to me Kohl is the best."

There was relief too from Kohl's coalition partners, the centrist Free Democrats and the Bavarian Christian Social Union, who had been urging him to declare his candidacy early to rally support in the coalition and put pressure on the opposition SPD.

Kohl, already post-war Germany's longest-serving chancellor, took office in 1982 and has defeated four SPD challengers since then. Only Count Otto von Bismarck, who was chancellor for 19 years and two months in the 19th century, has held power longer.

But Kohl's failure this year to marshal his party and coalition decisively behind major tax and pensions reform projects, and above all a rise in unemployment to its highest level since 1933, have taken their toll in public opinion polls.

This week's Emnid survey gave the CDU and FDP together 42 percent compared to 47 percent for the SPD and their potential allies, the Greens. The Forsa group gave the government only 39 percent compared to 52 percent for the opposition.
In an unrepresentative poll of 60,000 viewers who called the private television station RTL, 67.5 percent said Kohl should not stand again against 32.5 percent who said he should.
Kohl had repeatedly dodged questions about his 1998 plans since quickly retreating from an unguarded comment in 1994 that he did not plan to govern into the next century.
But in the interview, an annual event in which Kohl usually unveils the fruit of 10 days of contemplation in his Alpine retreat, he beamed when asked if he planned to run again.
"A very clear yes," he said. "I will stand again if my party and political friends want that...I want to pursue the necessary reforms."
The move was certain to put pressure on the SPD to declare who will stand against Kohl.
SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine is first in line for his party's nomination. But he has already lost to Kohl once in 1990, and is running behind him in opinion surveys.
Another SPD leader, Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, consistently runs ahead of Kohl in popularity polls but is less well loved within the left-leaning SPD itself.
